rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed while reducing gradient steepness to measure how the four critical pairs respond. The first run's early final peak suggests this diagnostic gradient should remain close to the ten-minute target.
The shallower gradient resolved most of the cluster but left one nearly coeluting pair. Raise temperature while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity changes and shorten retention.

Test a five-degree reduction from the best method to shift the remaining close pair while preserving the strong separation of the early cluster. The current retention-time margin should keep the last peak below ten minutes.

Return to the best temperature and slightly steepen the gradient to test whether the remaining close pair separates through its differing slope response. This also shortens the run; monitor the early pair currently just above R = 1.5.

The best method narrowly misses full resolution, while simply lengthening the gradient trades one critical pair against another. Raise the starting organic fraction by one grid step to adjust selectivity and slightly reduce gradient steepness, with ample retention for the first peak.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 6 to improve the early close pairs without consuming the later pair's resolution margin. The narrowed endpoint remains safely above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of about 0.41.

Injection 7 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention, with a slightly shallower slope to help preserve the marginal early-pair resolutions.

Reduce the slope at the higher starting fraction to recover separation in the early cluster while retaining some of the time savings. The later close pair has resolution margin to trade; injection 7 remains the maximum-score fallback.

The high-temperature region shows a tradeoff between critical pairs, so explore low-temperature selectivity for an alternative fully resolved method. Use a steeper gradient to offset increased retention, while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Lengthen the low-temperature gradient by one step to test whether the coeluting pair responds to slope. The last peak should remain below ten minutes, allowing a potentially fully resolved alternative without a time penalty.

Test a modest temperature increase against injection 10 to shift the nearly coeluting pair without lengthening the run. This explores a faster alternative while preserving injection 7 as the proven maximum-CRF method.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to change the low-temperature cluster's selectivity while limiting retention time. The first peak in injection 12 eluted near 0.27 organic, making 0.25 a useful starting-window probe; injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Substantially reduce the slope to separate the nearly coeluting cluster, following the slope sensitivity seen at low temperature. The 6.19-minute last peak leaves room for this longer gradient without necessarily exceeding the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Lower temperature to improve the final close pair, and slightly lengthen the gradient to help preserve separation in the central cluster. This tests a second fully resolved selectivity region while injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark.
Shorten the newly fully resolved low-temperature method by one gradient-time step to trade excess resolution for speed. Its minimum R of 2.06 provides useful margin before reaching the 1.5 threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten the low-temperature separation, while narrowing the gradient window to help protect the marginal central pair. The final fraction remains above the observed last-peak elution fraction, reducing the risk of a long hold.

Return to the fastest maximum-score region and increase gradient steepness slightly relative to injection 7. This intermediate slope tests whether retention can be shortened while keeping both marginal early pairs at R ≥ 1.5.

Injection 18 places the fastest proven region near its resolution boundary, so retain injection 7 as the benchmark. Test a steeper low-temperature gradient at the higher starting fraction to see whether the central pair separates on the opposite side of its elution-order crossover, with a shorter run.

Raise both solvent endpoints by one step while preserving slope to test whether the central pair separates further on this faster selectivity branch. Injection 19 has only one unresolved pair and useful resolution margin elsewhere, making this a promising route to a shorter maximum-score method.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-time step, using its minimum R of 1.85 as margin. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to measure the speed–resolution tradeoff directly.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the resolution boundary of the fastest fully resolved method. The two marginal pairs may fall below 1.5; if so, injection 21 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Test a lower starting fraction with a steeper gradient to shift the central-pair selectivity while targeting a shorter separation. Injection 21 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method; this probe checks whether a different solvent window can overcome its slope limit.

Shift the fastest fully resolved method's solvent window upward while preserving gradient slope to test further retention-time savings. This may change the central elution order, so injection 21 remains the fastest proven maximum-score benchmark.

Make the higher-starting-fraction gradient shallower to recover the single unresolved central pair while testing whether its retention-time advantage can be preserved. Injection 21 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method if this final refinement falls short.
